essays.stem: Explain how you would plan a formal investigation report into repeated weld defects: agreeing the terms of reference, choosing how to gather evidence, and setting a timetable.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would meet the person who asked for the report and agree the terms of reference: the purpose (to find why porosity keeps appearing, for example), the scope (which jobs, welders and dates), who will read it, and when it is due. Next I would plan how to gather evidence. Primary evidence would be the inspection records, the electrode oven log, the welding settings, photographs, and short interviews with the welders and the store keeper. I might also re-test some samples. Secondary sources would include the WPS and the maker's data. Then I would set a timetable working back from the deadline: days for collecting evidence, for analysing it, for writing the draft, for review by the supervisor, and for the final copy. I would also plan the headings, so I know what evidence each section needs, and agree who must approve the report.
markingPoints: Agrees purpose, scope, readers and deadline (terms of reference)
Plans primary evidence: records, logs, photos, interviews, tests
Uses secondary sources such as the WPS and maker's data
Sets a timetable back from the deadline, including review time
Plans headings and agrees who approves the report

essays.stem: A trainee was burned when a gas hose split during oxy-fuel cutting. Explain how you would investigate the incident and find the root cause, and how the investigation report should be set out.
essays.modelAnswer: First the area is made safe, the trainee gets first aid, and the hose and torch are kept as evidence without being changed. I would photograph the scene and the hose, take short statements from the trainee and witnesses in their own words, and collect the equipment inspection log, the hose's age and the training records. To find the root cause I would ask 'why?' step by step: the hose split because it was worn; it was worn because it was not replaced; it was not replaced because the pre-use check was not done or not recorded. The report would have a title page, a summary, an introduction with the scope, the method, the findings (the facts in time order, with photos), the analysis and root cause, conclusions, and clear recommendations with a person responsible and a date, such as a hose replacement schedule. Personal and medical details are kept confidential.
markingPoints: Makes safe, gives first aid, keeps the evidence unchanged
Gathers photos, statements, logs and training records
Uses a method such as the five whys to reach the root cause
Sets out the report: summary, introduction, method, findings, analysis, conclusions, recommendations
Recommendations have an owner and a date; confidential details protected

essays.stem: Explain how to choose and present data in a report using tables and graphs. Give an example of when you would use a table, a bar chart, a line graph and a Pareto chart.
essays.modelAnswer: Data should be shown in the way that makes the point clearest for the reader. A table is best when readers need exact figures, such as the leg sizes measured on 20 fillet welds. A bar chart compares amounts between groups, such as the number of rejected welds for each of four welders. A line graph shows change over time, such as the monthly reject rate over a year. A Pareto chart puts the causes in order from largest to smallest with a running total, so it shows which few causes, such as porosity and undercut, make up most of the problems. Every table and graph needs a number, a clear title, labelled axes with units, and a source. The scale should start at zero unless there is a good reason, so changes are not exaggerated. The text should say what each chart shows, and long raw data goes in an appendix.
markingPoints: Table for exact figures, with an example
Bar chart for comparing groups, with an example
Line graph for change over time, with an example
Pareto chart for the main causes, with an example
Numbers, titles, labelled axes, units, honest scales, text explains each chart

essays.stem: Explain the difference between findings, conclusions and recommendations, and write one example of each for a report on porosity in MIG welds.
essays.modelAnswer: Findings are the facts that were found or measured, with no opinion added. Conclusions are what the findings mean, worked out from the evidence. Recommendations say what should be done about it, by whom and by when. Example finding: 'Porosity was found in 14 of 60 MIG welds made in bay 3 between 5 and 16 October. The shop door beside bay 3 was open and a fan was blowing across the bay on those days.' Example conclusion: 'The most likely cause of the porosity was the draught from the fan and open door blowing the shielding gas away from the weld.' Example recommendation: 'The workshop supervisor will fit welding screens round bay 3 and move the fan by 30 October, and the team leader will check the reject rate for the following month.' Keeping these three apart lets the reader see the evidence before the opinion.
markingPoints: Findings are facts measured or seen
Conclusions are what the facts mean
Recommendations are actions with an owner and a date
Gives a correct example of each for MIG porosity
Explains why they are kept separate

essays.stem: Write a short executive summary (about 100–150 words) for a report recommending that the Centre buys a plasma cutting machine for sheet work. Then explain what makes your summary effective.
essays.modelAnswer: Summary: 'This report looks at whether the Centre should buy a plasma cutter for cutting sheet up to 12 mm. At present sheet is cut by hand with oxy-fuel, which gives rough edges and wide heat-affected areas, and needs about 6 hours of grinding each week. A trial with a hired plasma cutter in October cut sheet three times faster, with clean edges and almost no grinding. The machine would cost about J$650 000 plus GCT at the current rate, with running costs lower than oxy-fuel gas. Savings in time and gas would repay it in about two years. We recommend buying one machine, with training for two instructors, before the next intake.' It is effective because it states the purpose, the problem, the key evidence, the costs and the recommendation in plain words, so a busy reader can decide without reading the whole report.
markingPoints: States the purpose and the problem
Gives the key evidence in brief, with figures
Gives the cost, with GCT at the current rate
Gives a clear recommendation
Explains why it is effective: short, plain, enough to decide on

essays.stem: Explain how you would make a technical report clear and easy to read for readers whose first language is not English, or who will read it on a phone.
essays.modelAnswer: I would use short sentences with one idea each, and everyday words instead of long or fancy ones. Each trade term would be explained the first time it is used, and short forms written out in full first, with a glossary if there are many. I would use the active voice, such as 'The inspector checked the welds', and keep to the same word for the same thing. Headings and numbered sections help readers find their way, and short paragraphs are easier on a small screen. Lists and simple tables can replace long paragraphs. Photos with captions and simple sketches show what words cannot. Numbers are written with their units, using metric first. For phone readers I would put the key points and recommendations at the top, keep tables narrow, and send a file type that opens on any phone. Finally, I would ask someone from the readership to read a draft.
markingPoints: Short sentences, everyday words, active voice
Explains terms and short forms; glossary if needed; consistent words
Headings, short paragraphs, lists and simple tables
Photos, captions, sketches; units with every number
Phone-friendly layout with key points first; tests the draft on a reader

essays.stem: Explain how version control, review and approval work for a technical report, and why they matter on a contract job.
essays.modelAnswer: Version control means each draft gets a version number and date, for example v0.1, v0.2, and the issued copy v1.0. A short change table at the front shows what changed in each version and who changed it. The file name also shows the version. Review means another competent person, such as the supervisor or an inspector, checks the draft for accuracy, missing facts, clear wording and correct figures, and the writer answers each comment. Approval means the person with authority signs the report before it is issued. Only approved versions go to the customer, and old versions are marked as replaced. On a contract job this matters because the customer, inspectors and the team may make decisions or payments based on the report. If people work from different versions, mistakes, disputes and extra cost can follow. A clear record also shows who said what and when, if questions come up later.
markingPoints: Version numbers, dates and a change record
Review by a competent person; comments answered
Approval and signature before issue; old versions marked
Explains risks of people using different versions
Explains the value of the record on a contract job

essays.stem: Describe how to use photographs, sketches and drawings as evidence in a report so that they are accurate and useful.
essays.modelAnswer: Photographs should be taken at the time, in good light, with a ruler or tape in the shot to show size, and with a wider photo to show where the close-up was taken. They should not be edited in a way that changes what they show. Each photo gets a number and a caption saying what it shows, where and when, and the text refers to it by number. The original files are kept. Sketches are useful to show positions, such as where on a frame each faulty weld was found; they should be neat, labelled, and marked 'not to scale' if they are not. Drawings from the job should be copied with their number and revision, and marked up clearly, for example with weld numbers circled. Too many pictures can confuse the reader, so only those that support a finding are put in the body, and others go in an appendix.
markingPoints: Photos taken at the time, with scale and a wide view, not altered
Numbered captions saying what, where and when; text refers to them
Originals kept
Sketches labelled and marked 'not to scale' if needed
Drawings with number and revision; extra pictures in an appendix

essays.stem: Explain the legal and ethical duties of a report writer: accuracy, honesty, confidentiality and record keeping. Give an example of a problem for each.
essays.modelAnswer: Accuracy means the facts and figures are correct and checked. If a weld size is typed wrongly, a weak structure could be accepted. Honesty means reporting all the findings, including mistakes and bad news, and not changing figures. If a test failure is left out, the customer could be put at risk and the Centre could face legal action. Confidentiality means personal details, such as an injured trainee's medical information, and a customer's prices or drawings, are only shared with people who need them. Sending an incident report with medical details to a supplier would break this. Record keeping means reports and their evidence are filed safely for the time the Centre or the contract says. If inspection records are lost, the Centre cannot prove the work was checked if a failure happens later. A writer who is pressured to change a report should raise it with a higher manager.
markingPoints: Accuracy, with an example of a problem
Honesty, with an example of a problem
Confidentiality, with an example of a problem
Record keeping, with an example of a problem
Says what to do if pressured to change a report

essays.stem: Describe what a non-conformance report (NCR) should contain, and how it is followed through to close-out.
essays.modelAnswer: An NCR is raised as soon as work or material that does not meet the requirement is found. It should contain an NCR number, the date, the job and drawing number with revision, the item, what the requirement is and what was found (with measurements and photos), who found it, and how many items are affected. The faulty items are tagged and kept apart. The next part records the decision on what to do, called the disposition: rework, repair to an approved method, use as is with the customer's written agreement, or scrap, and who approved it. Then the cause is found and a corrective action is planned, with a person responsible and a date. When the action is done, the item is inspected again and the result recorded. The NCR is closed only when the item is acceptable and the corrective action has been checked to see that it worked, and it is signed off and filed.
markingPoints: NCR details: number, date, job, drawing, requirement, what was found, evidence, quantity
Items tagged and kept apart
Disposition recorded and approved
Cause found and corrective action with owner and date
Re-inspection, check that the action worked, sign-off and filing

practical1.title: Investigate a staged weld quality problem and write a formal investigation report
practical1.brief: The assessor sets up a staged quality problem: a set of rejected weld samples with tags, copies of the electrode oven log, the machine settings sheets, inspection records and two short witness notes. As a group of 4–5, agree the terms of reference with the assessor (who acts as the manager), then gather and record the evidence: photograph and measure the samples, put the inspection results in a table, and make a Pareto chart or bar chart of the defects. Use the five whys or a fishbone diagram to find the most likely root cause. Then write a formal investigation report together, with a title page, executive summary, introduction and scope, method, findings, analysis, conclusions, recommendations (each with an owner and a date) and appendices. Each member writes and signs at least one section, and one member keeps the version record. The group presents the findings to the assessor in about 5 minutes. Photograph each stage and add the photos and the report to the group's practical.
materials: Staged weld samples with defect tags (set up by the assessor)
Copies of an oven log, settings sheets, inspection records and witness notes
Weld gauges, a steel rule and a camera or phone
A computer with a word processor and spreadsheet, or paper, graph paper and pens
A report template with the headings, and a version record sheet
photos: The agreed terms of reference, written down
The samples laid out with a ruler for scale
The data table of inspection results
The fishbone diagram or five-whys sheet
The draft report with review comments
The final report title page and version record
checklist: Helped agree the terms of reference and stayed within them
Gathered and recorded evidence accurately (measurements, photos with scale)
Helped build the data table and chart correctly
Took part in finding the root cause with a recognised method
Wrote and signed at least one section in clear, objective language
Recommendations are specific, with an owner and a date
Checked another member's section and answered comments on their own
Took part in presenting the findings
safety: Handle weld samples with gloves: edges can be sharp
Keep cables from computers and chargers tidy so nobody trips
Work in the classroom area, not near live welding
Keep personal details in the staged notes confidential

practical2.title: Prepare a feasibility report comparing two options for a workshop improvement, and present it
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a workshop problem and two possible solutions, with prices and facts to use (for example: fume extraction for four welding bays, either one central extraction unit or four portable units). As a group, plan the report, then compare the two options using a cost table in a spreadsheet (prices in J$, with GCT shown as a separate line at the current rate given by the assessor), a simple scoring table for things such as safety, running cost, space and ease of use, and a short risk list. Write a feasibility report with an executive summary, background, the options, the comparison, conclusions and a recommendation. Each member takes a role (for example costs, safety, writing, charts and editing) and writes or builds one part, and the whole group reviews the final draft. Present the recommendation to the assessor, who acts as the Centre manager and asks questions. Photograph each stage, including the computer screen at each step, and add the photos and the report to the group's practical.
materials: The problem brief, prices and facts from the assessor (prices marked as made up for the exercise)
A computer with a spreadsheet and word processor, or calculators and paper
A report template and a scoring sheet
Phone or camera for photos of the screens and the work
photos: The group's plan and the role of each member
The spreadsheet cost table on screen, with formulas shown
The draft report with review marks
checklist: Took a clear role and completed it
Worked out costs correctly in J$, with GCT shown separately at the given rate
Compared the options fairly, using the same measures for each
Wrote clear, objective text in plain language
The recommendation follows from the comparison
Reviewed the draft and helped correct errors
Answered the assessor's questions during the presentation
safety: Sit correctly at the computer and take short breaks from the screen
Keep cables tidy and drinks away from the computers
If the group visits the welding bays for facts, wear safety glasses and keep out of welding areas
Use only the prices and facts given; do not share Centre data outside the group
